questions.q: What is CoreDNS's job in a Kubernetes cluster?
options: It builds and pushes container images
It runs as a cluster add-on that answers DNS queries for Services and Pods, watching the API server for changes
questions.explain: CoreDNS runs in kube-system, is queried by every Pod automatically, and resolves Service/Pod names by watching the API server — no manual DNS records needed.

questions.q: What is the fully qualified DNS name for Northbridge's checkout Service running in the default namespace?
A Pod in the 'reporting' namespace needs to reach the checkout Service running in the 'default' namespace. Which call will NOT work?
questions.explain: The bare short name only resolves within the same namespace due to the kubelet's configured search domains. Calling across namespaces requires at least the namespace suffix, e.g. checkout.default.

questions.q: What does setting clusterIP: None on a Service change about its behavior?
options: It makes the Service unreachable from any Pod
DNS returns the individual IPs of every matching Pod instead of one load-balanced virtual IP — the headless Service pattern
It forces the Service to use NodePort instead
questions.explain: A headless Service (clusterIP: None) skips the single virtual IP and load-balancing; DNS resolution returns a record per backing Pod, which is how StatefulSets address individual replicas.

questions.q: Why does Northbridge's product-catalog code call 'http://checkout' instead of an IP address?
options: Because IP addresses are not supported inside containers
Because DNS lets the name resolve to whatever the Service's current ClusterIP is, decoupling the code from any specific address
Because HTTP requires a hostname by protocol specification
Because 'checkout' is faster to type than an IP
questions.explain: Calling by DNS name means the code never depends on a specific IP — DNS resolves to the Service's stable virtual IP, which itself routes to whichever Pods are currently healthy.
